items.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: And he had found a song he wrote with Harry Warren, “There Is No Music For Me” or I think the title was “There Is No Music For Me.” I’d never heard that song.

ctx.x: Well I’d done some things mostly with doing things for singers, you know Maxine Sullivan and just arranging stuff behind her. Because with singers it’s nice to have a little organized backing like we did tonight, we did those things behind Rebecca [Kilgore], it’s lovely. You know it makes all the difference because it gives it a nice little showcase setting for a singer. And I do like singers. A lot of musicians don’t like singers, but I like

it because you’re hearing the lyrics, and it’s good to work, I think there’s a very healthy cabaret scene. That’s one thing — I mean the jazz scene to me is not particularly, say interesting, it’s not, it doesn’t interest me much today, I mean what’s going on in contemporary ways, which may sound a bit fuddy duddy to you, but I don’t believe that anything that’s thirty, forty years old is particularly old. Perhaps we Europeans, we have a different time concept. But you know to me Jerome Kern and these melodies…
Yeah. Unfortunately it seems like the composers have delved into the harmonic schemes of Pop and Rock ‘n Roll—
